chapters.title: Container Process Model
chapters.summary: Start with the smallest useful building block: a container whose lifetime is controlled by one process.
chapters.goal: See that a container lives while its PID 1 process lives. Compare a long-lived sleep infinity process with a command override.
chapters.adds: Creates public-a-test without a network. This is the seed service later chapters place into the lab.

steps.title: Start the seed service
steps.copy: Bring up the first stage without building a network yet.

steps.title: Inspect the process table
steps.copy: Confirm that Docker is keeping the service alive with sleep infinity.

steps.title: Read PID 1 directly
steps.copy: Look at the command line of the first process in the container namespace.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 01 exec public-a-test sh -c 'tr "\0" " " </proc/1/cmdline; printf "\n"'

checkpoint.question: What should `/proc/1/cmdline` contain?
checkpoint.expected: PID 1 is sleep infinity. A command that exits normally gives Docker an exit status and the service stops.

breakIt.copy: Run a one-shot container with true and compare it with the long-running service.

chapters.takeaway: A container is a process boundary, not a virtual machine.

chapters.title: CIDR and Bridge Networks
chapters.summary: Give the lab real boundaries with six user-defined Docker bridge networks and explicit /24 address ranges.
chapters.goal: Create six user-defined bridge networks with explicit /24 CIDRs and fixed container addresses.
chapters.adds: Attaches public-a-test to public_a and creates five more diagnostic containers plus five more bridge networks. No router exists yet.

steps.title: Start all six boundaries
steps.copy: Create the cumulative stage and confirm the six diagnostic services are running.

steps.title: Inventory Docker networks
steps.copy: Check that public, app, and database bridges exist as separate local networks.

steps.title: Inspect one interface and route
steps.copy: Read the address and directly connected route inside the app tier.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 02 exec public-a-test ip addr
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 02 exec app-a-test ip route

checkpoint.question: Why can containers on different bridges not communicate directly?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 02 exec app-a-test ip route
checkpoint.expected: Each container has only its local connected network. There is no router connecting app_a to app_b or any other bridge yet.

breakIt.copy: Try a cross-network request before a router exists. Record the failure without adding a route.

chapters.takeaway: A bridge is a boundary until a device deliberately connects it.

chapters.title: Network Namespaces and Interfaces
chapters.summary: Look inside the Linux networking view Docker created for one container before introducing routing.
chapters.goal: Identify the loopback, container interface, IP address, connected route, neighbor table, and how neighbors change after traffic.
chapters.adds: Adds no topology. This chapter inspects the six isolated bridges created in chapter 02.

steps.title: Start the inspection stage
steps.copy: Bring up the previous topology and list its services.

steps.title: Inspect the namespace
steps.copy: Read the interfaces and route table inside app-a-test.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 03 exec app-a-test ip addr
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 03 exec app-a-test ip route

steps.title: Generate a neighbor entry
steps.copy: Inspect the neighbor table, ping the local Docker gateway, then inspect it again.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 03 exec app-a-test ip neigh
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 03 exec app-a-test ip neigh

checkpoint.question: What changed after pinging 10.10.11.1?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 03 exec app-a-test ip neigh
checkpoint.expected: Traffic can populate the neighbor cache. It is evidence of learned next-hop information, not a complete inventory of every device.

breakIt.copy: Ask Linux how it would route toward another subnet before a router exists.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 03 exec app-a-test ip route get 10.10.12.10

chapters.takeaway: Every container starts with its own local networking environment.

chapters.title: Linux Capabilities
chapters.summary: Permission is part of the network. Root inside a container still needs the specific capability to change routes.
chapters.goal: Understand why root is restricted, what capabilities are, why route changes require CAP_NET_ADMIN, and why permission does not make a route valid.
chapters.adds: Builds the reusable lab-tools image with iproute2, iptables, tcpdump, curl, netcat, python3, and bind-tools.

steps.title: Build the diagnostic image
steps.copy: Create the reusable Alpine-based image used by later routing experiments.

steps.title: Predict the permission boundary
steps.copy: Start without NET_ADMIN, enter as root, and compare identity with privileged operations.

steps.title: Add the network capability
steps.copy: Repeat the route operation with the capability granted by Compose.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 04 exec app-a-test ip route

checkpoint.question: What did NET_ADMIN change?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 04 exec app-a-test ip route
checkpoint.expected: It grants permission to perform network administration. It does not create interfaces, routes, next hops, forwarding, firewall permission, or a listener by itself.

breakIt.copy: Remove the capability in a disposable container and repeat the route command. Compare the permission error with a later connectivity failure.

chapters.takeaway: Permission to configure a route is not the same as a valid routed network path.

chapters.title: Multi-Homed Router Container
chapters.summary: Introduce a Layer-3 device attached to all six bridges, then observe the connected routes Linux creates for it.
chapters.goal: Build a router container with one IP on each subnet, connected routes for every subnet, and IPv4 forwarding enabled.
chapters.adds: Adds lab-router with .2 on public_a, public_b, app_a, app_b, db_a, and db_b.

steps.title: Start the router stage
steps.copy: Bring up the six diagnostic containers plus lab-router.

steps.title: Inspect every interface
steps.copy: Enter the router and find one address in each lab subnet.

steps.title: Read connected routes
steps.copy: The kernel learns routes automatically because each network is directly attached.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05 exec lab-router ip route
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05 exec lab-router sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward

checkpoint.question: What does the router know automatically?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05 exec lab-router ip route
checkpoint.expected: It knows all six directly connected /24 subnets. Forwarding must still be enabled before it can pass packets between interfaces.

breakIt.copy: Inspect the router before forwarding is enabled and compare endpoint traffic with traffic that must cross interfaces.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05 exec lab-router ip addr

chapters.takeaway: A router is an endpoint on every subnet and a forwarder between them.

chapters.title: Static Routing
chapters.summary: Teach client containers which local router address to use when a destination lives on a remote subnet.
chapters.goal: Identify missing remote routes, choose a valid local next hop, inspect route selection, and distinguish forward from return paths.
chapters.adds: Adds runtime routes to the six diagnostic containers through lab-router. The optional 05B chain remains a separate lab.

steps.title: Observe the chapter 05 baseline
steps.copy: Start the router topology and inspect app-a-test before adding remote routes.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05 exec app-a-test ip route
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05 exec app-a-test ip route get 10.10.12.10

steps.title: Test the missing path
steps.copy: A lab-router exists, but app-a-test still uses Docker default routing. Confirm the expected failure.

steps.title: Apply and inspect the overlay
steps.copy: Start chapter 06 and verify the route uses the router address on app_a.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 06 exec app-a-test ip route get 10.10.12.10

checkpoint.question: Why is 10.10.11.2 a valid next hop from app-a-test?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 06 exec app-a-test ip route
checkpoint.expected: The next hop must be reachable on the sender local network. app-a-test can reach lab-router at .2 on app_a, not the router address on a different subnet.

breakIt.copy: Delete a destination return route and observe a connection that reaches the router but cannot complete.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 06 exec app-b-test ip route

chapters.takeaway: Routing is a two-way contract: the request path and the return path must both exist.

chapters.title: Packet Tracing
chapters.summary: Turn a route-table prediction into evidence by watching ingress, forwarded egress, and the reply on the router.
chapters.goal: Use tcpdump to prove where a packet enters and leaves the router.
chapters.adds: Adds no service. It adds an observation workflow using the lab-tools image from chapter 04.

steps.title: Start the routed topology
steps.copy: Use the accumulated stage through chapter 07.

steps.title: Capture on every interface
steps.copy: Run the capture in one terminal so the router can show both sides of the flow.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 07 exec lab-router tcpdump -i any -nn icmp

steps.title: Generate the packet
steps.copy: From another terminal, ping app-b from public-a and match each capture line to the route.

checkpoint.question: What four events should appear?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 07 exec lab-router tcpdump -i any -nn icmp
checkpoint.expected: Ingress from public_a, forwarded egress to app_b, reply ingress from app_b, and reply egress to public_a.

breakIt.copy: Capture only one router interface and explain why half of the conversation disappears.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 07 exec lab-router tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp

chapters.takeaway: A packet path is a sequence of observable interface events.

chapters.title: Stateful Firewalling
chapters.summary: Replace unrestricted forwarding with a default-deny policy and allow only the ports the application design requires.
chapters.goal: Allow required application flows while explaining FORWARD, conntrack, rule order, and the difference between DROP and refusal.
chapters.adds: Allows established return traffic, public-to-app TCP 8000, app-to-database TCP 5432, and database replication TCP 5432.

steps.title: Start the firewall stage
steps.copy: Bring up the router with its forwarding policy applied by the entrypoint.

steps.title: Read rules and counters
steps.copy: Inspect the rule order before generating traffic.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 08 exec lab-router iptables -L FORWARD -n -v --line-numbers
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 08 exec lab-router iptables -S FORWARD

steps.title: Compare permitted and dropped flows
steps.copy: A timeout indicates a drop; a refusal means a host was reached but no service listened.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 08 exec lab-router iptables -L FORWARD -n -v --line-numbers

checkpoint.question: Why is one ESTABLISHED,RELATED rule enough for replies?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 08 exec lab-router iptables -S FORWARD
checkpoint.expected: Conntrack remembers the flow state, so permitted return traffic can match the state rule instead of needing a second reverse-direction allow rule.

breakIt.copy: Flush FORWARD and compare a timeout caused by DROP with a refusal caused by a reachable host without a listener.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 08 exec lab-router iptables -F FORWARD

chapters.takeaway: The route chooses the path; the firewall chooses whether the flow may use it.

chapters.title: Private Networks
chapters.summary: Mark the application and database bridges as internal so their normal Docker egress path disappears.
chapters.goal: Make application and database networks private at the Docker bridge layer.
chapters.adds: Sets internal: true on app_a, app_b, db_a, and db_b. The lab router can still route between attached internal zones.

steps.title: Inspect the rendered Compose
steps.copy: Confirm which networks now carry the internal flag.

steps.title: Read the private route table
steps.copy: Inspect app-a-test before a NAT gateway exists.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 09 exec app-a-test ip route

steps.title: Keep the distinction clear
steps.copy: A private bridge is not the same thing as a firewall policy. The router still controls forwarded lab traffic.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 09 exec app-a-test ip route get 10.10.21.10

checkpoint.question: What disappears before chapter 10?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 09 exec app-a-test ip route
checkpoint.expected: There is no useful direct path to an external address, while an explicit route through lab-router can still reach another lab subnet when policy allows it.

breakIt.copy: Try to reach a public address from app-a-test before NAT. Record the route and failure without changing the stack.

chapters.takeaway: Private means no default external attachment, not invisible or unreachable from every lab container.

chapters.title: NAT Gateway
chapters.summary: Separate routing from address translation and provide controlled egress for private application networks.
chapters.goal: Follow a private packet to the NAT gateway, then observe MASQUERADE rewrite the source after routing chooses the interface.
chapters.adds: Attaches nat-gateway to both app networks and nat_public. App default routes point to it and the gateway MASQUERADEs app traffic.

steps.title: Inspect the selected route
steps.copy: Ask app-a which next hop and interface it will use for the public NAT network.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 10 exec app-a-test ip route get 10.10.30.10

steps.title: Inspect translation rules
steps.copy: Read POSTROUTING before generating the request.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 10 exec nat-gateway iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n -v

steps.title: Run the egress check
steps.copy: Run the repository NAT test and compare the rule counters afterward.

checkpoint.question: What happens first: routing or NAT?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 10 exec app-a-test ip route get 10.10.30.10
checkpoint.expected: Routing chooses the egress interface and next hop first. MASQUERADE rewrites the source afterward; it does not choose a route.

breakIt.copy: Delete the NAT gateway default route while leaving MASQUERADE configured. The counters should stay unchanged.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 10 exec nat-gateway ip route

chapters.title: Docker DNS
chapters.summary: Separate raw IP connectivity from hostname resolution inside user-defined Docker networks.
chapters.goal: Distinguish Docker embedded DNS, service discovery, upstream DNS, routing, and TCP reachability.
chapters.adds: Adds no topology. It inspects the accumulated stack and compares IP and DNS tests.

steps.title: Inspect the resolver
steps.copy: Read the resolver endpoint Docker puts inside app-a-test.

steps.title: Resolve a service name
steps.copy: Ask Docker for a name that exists in the shared network view.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 11 exec app-a-test getent hosts postgres-primary

steps.title: Compare public DNS
steps.copy: Check a public hostname separately from service discovery.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 11 exec app-a-test getent hosts example.com
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 11 exec app-a-test ip route

checkpoint.question: If a raw IP works but a hostname fails, which layer is suspect?
checkpoint.expected: Investigate DNS first. Name resolution does not prove a route, firewall rule, listener, or application authentication will work.

breakIt.copy: Replace resolv.conf with a bad nameserver and compare a known IP request with a hostname request.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 11 exec app-a-test getent hosts example.com

chapters.takeaway: DNS answers an IP-name question; it does not prove the rest of the packet path.

chapters.title: Nginx Public Access
chapters.summary: Put an application-layer reverse proxy on each public subnet and route its upstream request to the matching private app.
chapters.goal: Expose the app through Nginx without placing the app itself on the public network.
chapters.adds: Turns the app diagnostics into Python HTTP servers and adds nginx-a/nginx-b at .3 on the public bridges.

steps.title: Check the public path
steps.copy: Request the public A and public B proxy addresses from their matching clients.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 12 exec public-a-test curl -sS http://10.10.1.3
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 12 exec public-b-test curl -sS http://10.10.2.3

steps.title: Validate Nginx config
steps.copy: Let Nginx validate its configuration before interpreting network failures.

steps.title: Follow the two connections
steps.copy: Client-to-Nginx and Nginx-to-app are separate requests with different boundaries.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 12 exec nginx-a curl -sS http://10.10.11.10:8000

checkpoint.question: What does proxy success prove?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 12 exec public-a-test curl -sS http://10.10.1.3
checkpoint.expected: The public client can reach Nginx and Nginx can reach app-a-test:8000 through the router. It does not mean direct public-to-app traffic is allowed.

breakIt.copy: Stop nginx-a and compare public A failure with a direct app request from the router.

chapters.takeaway: A reverse proxy terminates one connection and creates another.

chapters.title: PostgreSQL Primary
chapters.summary: Add a writable database to the database tier and validate the path at TCP, SQL, process, and authentication layers.
chapters.goal: Validate application-to-database routing at TCP and SQL layers without confusing network filtering with pg_hba.conf.
chapters.adds: Adds postgres-primary at 10.10.21.20, return routes to both app networks and the future replica, and replication settings for chapter 15.

steps.title: Test transport reachability
steps.copy: Use netcat to prove the TCP handshake before testing SQL.

steps.title: Run a SQL query
steps.copy: The database layer is a separate check after the port is open.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 13 exec postgres-primary psql -U labadmin -d labdb -c 'SELECT version();'

steps.title: Inspect the server process
steps.copy: Confirm the primary is writable and ready for a future standby.

checkpoint.question: What does nc prove, and what does it not prove?
checkpoint.expected: It proves a TCP handshake. It does not prove PostgreSQL authentication, pg_hba.conf acceptance, or SQL correctness.

breakIt.copy: Remove the primary route to app_a and observe the client-side connection hang despite the router forward rule.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 13 exec postgres-primary ip route

chapters.takeaway: iptables decides whether the packet crosses; PostgreSQL decides whether the session is accepted.

chapters.title: PostgreSQL Processes and Job Control
chapters.summary: Connect the container PID 1 model to PostgreSQL main, background, and client backend processes.
chapters.goal: Understand how one database service becomes a coordinated process family and how shell job control differs from container persistence.
chapters.adds: Adds no topology. The primary from chapter 13 is the process laboratory.

steps.title: List the PostgreSQL process family
steps.copy: See the main server, checkpointer, WAL writer, autovacuum, and backend processes.

steps.title: Identify your SQL backend
steps.copy: Ask PostgreSQL which operating-system process serves the current session.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 14 exec postgres-primary psql -U labadmin -d labdb -c 'SELECT pg_backend_pid();'

steps.title: Practice shell job control
steps.copy: Use a disposable shell for Ctrl-Z, bg, jobs, and fg. Do not background the database process itself.

checkpoint.question: What happens if one client backend dies?
checkpoint.expected: The PostgreSQL server and background processes remain alive. The client session is one process in a larger supervised service.

breakIt.copy: Kill one client backend from a test connection and explain why the server remains healthy.

chapters.takeaway: Shell job control is not a replacement for a supervised container process.

chapters.title: Physical Streaming Replication
chapters.summary: Copy the primary cluster into a second database subnet, then observe WAL stream and replay on a read-only standby.
chapters.goal: Initialize a standby with pg_basebackup and observe WAL streaming across the routed database subnets.
chapters.adds: Adds postgres-replica at 10.10.22.20 and intentionally starts it as sleep infinity so it cannot initialize a conflicting cluster first.

steps.title: Prepare the standby directory
steps.copy: Enter the replica, clear the target directory, and restore PostgreSQL ownership and permissions.

steps.title: Copy the physical cluster
steps.copy: Run pg_basebackup with streaming WAL and generated standby configuration.

steps.title: Start and verify recovery
steps.copy: Start PostgreSQL on the replica and compare recovery and replication state.

checkpoint.question: What proves this is streaming replication?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 15 exec postgres-replica psql -U labadmin -d labdb -c 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();'
checkpoint.expected: The replica returns t, the primary returns f, and the primary reports the replica as streaming. Inserts on the primary appear on the read-only replica.

breakIt.copy: Run pg_basebackup against a non-empty data directory and explain why the replica must not initialize its own unrelated cluster first.

chapters.takeaway: Base backup gives the starting state; WAL streaming gives the ongoing state.

chapters.title: Runtime Configuration Persistence
chapters.summary: Move manual routes and replica bootstrap into idempotent entrypoints so recreation converges on the same runtime state.
chapters.goal: Make routes and replica bootstrap repeatable with ip route replace, a named volume, PG_VERSION, and exec.
chapters.adds: The replica entrypoint waits for the primary, runs pg_basebackup only for an empty volume, writes a password file, and delegates to the official PostgreSQL entrypoint.

steps.title: Start the persistent stage
steps.copy: Build and wait for the complete stack.

steps.title: Verify standby state
steps.copy: Check the replica and primary from inside their containers.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 16 exec postgres-replica psql -U labadmin -d labdb -c 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();'
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 16 exec postgres-primary psql -U labadmin -d labdb -c 'SELECT client_addr, state FROM pg_stat_replication;'

steps.title: Recreate and compare
steps.copy: Restart the replica and inspect logs for readiness, standby mode, and WAL streaming.

checkpoint.question: Which state survives recreation?
checkpoint.expected: A clean volume performs one base backup. A restart keeps the cluster and reapplies routes without copying the database again.

breakIt.copy: Compare a route added manually in a disposable diagnostic container with a route restored by the entrypoint.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 16 exec postgres-replica ip route

chapters.takeaway: Persistent behavior belongs in the image, entrypoint, Compose file, or volume.

chapters.title: Failure Testing and Cloud Mapping
chapters.summary: Turn the whole lab into a repeatable test surface and learn to locate the first layer where behavior changes.
chapters.goal: Validate the final architecture, remove one dependency at a time, and map the result to VPC concepts without treating Docker as a managed cloud service.
chapters.adds: Adds no new service. It adds verification scripts and completes the final teaching loop.

steps.title: Start from a passing checkpoint
steps.copy: Bring up the final cumulative stage and wait for services to be ready.

steps.title: Run focused checks
steps.copy: Validate routing, firewalling, NAT, and replication separately.

steps.title: Change one dependency
steps.copy: Record the symptom, identify the first layer that changed, restore, and rerun every check.

checkpoint.question: What is the diagnostic order?
checkpoint.expected: Route, neighbor, packet capture, firewall, TCP listener, application protocol, then authentication. Map Docker bridge to VPC subnet, router to routing fabric, and the replica to a standby.

breakIt.copy: Run one failure at a time: delete an app return route, change FORWARD to ACCEPT, stop nginx-a, stop the primary, or remove the replica WAL connection.

chapters.takeaway: A useful system makes failure visible, local, and recoverable.

alternateChapter.title: Routed Network Chain
alternateChapter.summary: A standalone chain of four networks joined by three two-interface routers.
alternateChapter.goal: Identify connected routes, choose static next hops, trace multiple Layer-3 hops, and validate the return path.
alternateChapter.adds: Uses net_1 through net_4 at 10.50.1.0/24 through 10.50.4.0/24 with lab-router-1, lab-router-2, and lab-router-3.

steps.title: Start the alternate topology
steps.copy: This lab is standalone and is not combined with chapter 05 standard topology.

steps.title: Read each hop
steps.copy: Inspect the router interfaces and connected routes across the four networks.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05b exec lab-router-1 ip route
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05b exec lab-router-2 ip route
bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05b exec lab-router-3 ip route

steps.title: Trace the chain
steps.copy: Follow shell-1 to shell-3 through two Layer-3 hops and verify the reverse path.

checkpoint.question: How many hops separate shell-1 and shell-3?
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05b exec shell-1 ip route get 10.50.3.10
checkpoint.expected: The packet crosses lab-router-1 and lab-router-2. The reply must cross them in reverse.

breakIt.copy: Remove one static route in the chain and observe the hop where traffic stops.
commands: bash scripts/compose-stage.sh 05b exec shell-1 ip route

alternateChapter.takeaway: A multi-hop route is a series of correct local next-hop decisions.

courseModules.title: Foundation
courseModules.copy: Build the process, bridge, namespace, and permission mental models before routing anything.

courseModules.title: Routing and packet flow
courseModules.copy: Introduce the router, teach endpoints their next hops, and prove the path with packet capture.

courseModules.title: Traffic control and egress
courseModules.copy: Apply stateful policy, make networks private, add NAT, and separate DNS from reachability.

courseModules.title: Service and data tier
courseModules.copy: Expose HTTP through Nginx, add PostgreSQL, build a standby, and make runtime state repeatable.

10.state: Private app networks / nat-gateway / nat_public egress network / MASQUERADE

prediction.question: Does MASQUERADE decide which interface a private packet should leave through?
choices: No, routing chooses the path first
prediction.explanation: Routing chooses the egress path. MASQUERADE then rewrites the source address for traffic leaving through the selected external interface.

11.state: No topology change / compare Docker DNS, upstream DNS, and raw IP reachability

prediction.question: A raw IP request works but the equivalent hostname lookup fails. Which layer should be investigated first?
prediction.explanation: Raw IP reachability already demonstrates that name resolution is not required for that path. Start at DNS before changing routing or firewall rules.

12.state: nginx-a/nginx-b on public subnets / Python HTTP apps on private app subnets

prediction.question: When Nginx reverse-proxies a request to app-a-test, is the client-to-Nginx TCP connection the same connection as Nginx-to-app?
prediction.explanation: Nginx terminates the client connection and creates an upstream connection. Each leg can fail at a different network boundary.

13.state: Writable PostgreSQL primary on db_a / app-to-database routing and database policy

prediction.question: `nc` successfully connects to TCP 5432. Does that prove PostgreSQL will accept the user and SQL query?
prediction.explanation: A TCP handshake proves transport reachability. PostgreSQL authentication, pg_hba.conf policy, database existence, and SQL correctness are later layers.

14.state: PostgreSQL primary unchanged / process family and shell job-control inspection

prediction.question: If one PostgreSQL client backend process exits, should the entire PostgreSQL server stop?
prediction.explanation: Client backends are members of a larger PostgreSQL process family. The main server and background processes continue serving other sessions.

15.state: Primary on db_a / manual standby bootstrap on db_b / WAL streaming

prediction.question: Can a replica begin from an unrelated PostgreSQL data directory and become a physical standby by receiving only new WAL records?
choices: No, it needs a compatible base state first
prediction.explanation: Physical replication needs the same underlying cluster state. pg_basebackup creates that starting point; WAL streaming advances it afterward.

16.state: Named PostgreSQL volume / idempotent entrypoints / routes reapplied on recreation

prediction.question: Will an `ip route add` performed manually inside a running container survive that container being recreated?
prediction.explanation: The network namespace is recreated with the container. Runtime routes must be expressed in startup logic or another persistent configuration mechanism.

17.state: Final cumulative stack / routing, firewall, NAT, HTTP, database, replication and failure checks

prediction.question: During a failure experiment, should you break several dependencies at once to reveal more problems quickly?
choices: No, change one dependency at a time
prediction.explanation: Controlled failure injection keeps cause and effect observable. Establish a passing baseline, change one dependency, locate the first changed layer, restore, and retest.

01.state: 1 seed container / no custom network yet

prediction.question: If PID 1 exits but another process still exists in the container namespace, does Docker keep the container running?
choices: Only if the process is root
prediction.explanation: Docker treats PID 1 as the lifecycle anchor. When that process exits, the container stops and the remaining processes do not keep it alive.

02.state: 6 bridge networks / 6 diagnostic containers / no router

prediction.question: After creating app_a and app_b as separate Docker bridges, can app-a-test reach app-b-test without adding a router?
prediction.explanation: Each bridge is its own Layer-2 boundary. The endpoints only know their connected network, and no Layer-3 device connects the two bridges yet.

03.state: 6 isolated bridges / inspect one container namespace at a time

prediction.question: Before app-a-test sends any traffic, should `ip neigh` already contain every container on its Docker network?
choices: No, neighbors are learned as needed
prediction.explanation: The neighbor table is runtime evidence of Layer-2 resolution. It is populated as destinations or next hops are actually used.

04.state: Reusable lab-tools image / capability experiments / six-network topology retained
